title: The services page a nonprofit actually needs
metaTitle: A nonprofit services page visitors can use
excerpt: Describe each program with an outcome, a boundary, and a next step in the visitor's words. Vague grids of hope and support do not help someone enroll or give.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, for a piece on giving each program a clear edge.
caption: A shoreline with a visible edge. A program list should be that distinct. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should each program block contain?
faqs.answer: An outcome someone could notice, a boundary, and a next step. The boundary covers who it is for, where and when it runs, and what you do not do. The step is apply, volunteer, give, or read, in the verb that matches that block.

faqs.question: Should participants and donors share one block?
faqs.answer: They can read the same facts. The steps should be visually separate, so a person seeking help is not funneled into a fundraising form. Write so participants are addressed as readers. A donor can still see how a gift is used, in one sentence.

faqs.question: What practical facts cannot be deferred?
faqs.answer: Place, time, cost to the participant, and whether the program is open or full. These make the work real. A beautiful description that omits them asks people to email for the basics. Many will not, and they will assume the program is fuzzy.

markdown:
A nonprofit services page lists the work in the language of a donor or a participant who is deciding whether the work is real. Each program needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The next step is to give, join, or read the program. A grid of vague capabilities, hope, empowerment, support, innovation, does not help anyone choose.

Call the page whatever your visitors call the work. Programs, services, what we do. The name can match the menu. The content has to be a set of distinct offers. If two blocks could swap their titles and nobody would notice, you have one program wearing two hats, or you have adjectives where the work should be.

## Name the program the way people ask for it

Use the words that show up in referrals, in voicemails, and in the way a participant introduces you to a friend. The Tuesday legal clinic. School food bags. The trail crew. The family membership. Internal strategy names and grant titles can stay in the grant file. The page should use the public name, the one a person can say without reading your strategic plan.

Lead with the program you can deliver now and that you most need people to find. A seasonal program can move up while it is open and move down, with a date, when it is closed. A closed program that still looks like the front door creates calls you cannot honor. Mark it closed, say when it returns, or take it off until it returns.

Group programs by the person they are for when the audiences differ. Help for participants. Ways to give time. Ways to give money. Those are different jobs, and a single mixed grid makes each audience wade through the others. If the list is short, simple headings are enough. You do not need a database. You need a reader to see their door in one scan.

Open the page with a sentence that places the organization. Who you serve, where, and the kind of work. Then the programs. A long welcome about your theory of change delays the list. The theory can live in one clause under a program, where it explains why that outcome is the one you chose.

## Outcome, boundary, and the next step

The outcome is what is true when the program has done its job for a person or a place. A will drafted. A week of dinners in the bag. A trail segment cleared and signed. A child enrolled for the session. Write the outcome as a result someone could notice. Inner transformation may be real and still be the wrong sentence for this block, because a stranger cannot tell whether you offer it.

The boundary is who it is for, where it happens, when it runs, and what you do not do. Age, geography, eligibility, language, the level of need you are set up for, and the needs you refer elsewhere. A boundary is care. It saves a person a trip across town for a service you will not be able to give them. It also shows a donor that the program is a specific instrument.

The next step matches the audience of that block. Join, apply, refer, volunteer, give, or read the fuller program page. One primary step. The others can be text links. "Learn more" is acceptable only when it leads to a page that itself has a real step. A chain of learn-more links is a maze.

Use the same order in every block. Outcome, boundary, next step. A case worker comparing options, or a donor comparing programs, can scan. Vary the facts. Keep the skeleton. A small staff can maintain a skeleton. They cannot maintain five different storytelling formats invented in five different board meetings.

## Participants and donors read the same block differently

Write the block so a participant is not spoken about as if they were absent. "Families can pick up boxes on Thursdays" includes the family as the reader. "We provide boxes to families" talks past them. You can still include a sentence a donor needs, about what the shift costs or how a gift is used, without changing the subject into an object.

Where a program should not share a door with fundraising, separate the steps visually. Apply here. If you want to fund this program, give here. A person seeking help should not have to decide whether they are a prospect before they can see the hours. Dignity is a layout decision as much as a writing decision.

Staff and volunteer blocks deserve the same structure. Outcome: what a volunteer shift accomplishes. Boundary: the training, the background check, the minimum commitment, who should not apply. Next step: the form or the information session. A volunteer page that is only enthusiasm produces no-shows. The boundary sets the expectation that makes a shift real.

Referral partners need a block or a note, if professionals are how people arrive. What you need in a referral, what you will send back, and what you cannot accept. A school counselor or a discharge planner is a buyer of a kind. They are deciding whether the work is real and whether sending someone to you is safe. Write for them in public. They are already forwarding your URL.

## Where, when, and what it costs to take part

Each program block should carry the practical facts even if a deeper page repeats them. Place, time, cost to the participant, and the current open or closed state. These are the facts that make the work real. A beautiful description that omits Thursdays and the address asks the reader to trust you and then email you for the basics. Many will not email. They will assume the program is fuzzy because the facts were fuzzy.

If the pricing page holds the full shape of fees and gifts, link it at the moment the block mentions money. Do not contradict it. Free on the services page and a materials fee at intake is a broken promise. Fix the fee or fix the sentence. Say "free to families, funded by gifts" if that is the model, and link the giving path for the donor who is reading over the participant's shoulder.

Capacity is part of the boundary. A clinic that is full should say it is full and how the wait list works. A program with room should say how to take a place. Leaving capacity unspoken forces every reader to inquire, and it forces people in crisis to inquire into a void. Publish the state. Update it on the rhythm the program actually changes. A monthly edit is enough for many organizations. A daily one is required for a shelter bed. Match the rhythm to the work.

Languages, accessibility of the building, and transit are boundaries too. A step-free entrance, a program offered in two languages, a site on a bus line. These facts decide whether a person can use what you offer. They belong in the block, not in a PDF titled "inclusion" that nobody opens.

## What you do not run

A short section under the list can say what you are not. You do not offer emergency housing. You do not take walk-in medical cases. You do not fundraise for individuals. Refer to a specific public resource when you have a responsible place to send people. A bare "we don't do that" without a pointer is colder than it needs to be, and a false pointer is worse. Only name partners you would call yourself.

This section protects the programs above it. It keeps the blocks from swelling with disclaimers. It also answers the donor who wondered whether their gift would be stretched across missions you do not have. A focused no makes the yes more believable.

Avoid a partner logo row in place of this clarity. Logos do not state a boundary. If a partnership changes what a participant can expect, write the sentence. The logo can sit beside it if the agreement includes the mark. Unexplained logos are decoration, and decoration is how a services page starts to look like a grant report cover.

## A page a board member can forward

The test of a block is forwarding. A board member, a volunteer, or a participant should be able to send one program to a friend and have it stand alone. The friend can see what happens, who it is for, and what to do. If the block only makes sense after a speech, it is still a speech.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for a clear purpose and for pages that help someone finish a real task. This page's purpose is to show which programs exist, who they are for, and how to enter. A block that cannot do that is a slogan, and it should come off.

Keep names stable between the page, the intake form, the receipt, and the way the phone is answered. If the site says "family table" and the staff say "the pantry," pick one public name and teach it internally. People in need should not have to translate your brand system while they are asking for a time and a place.

On a Hanabi project the page is a simple, editable structure. Outcome, boundary, next step, repeated in the same type and the same components, so a program lead can change the hours without waiting for a redesign. The studio designs and builds it. The staff keep it true. After launch, the current program sheets can live in the client portal next to logos and consent notes, so the public page and the internal sheet do not diverge in two folders.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) when you want that structure built around the programs you actually run. Bring the list of what is open this season, and the sentences intake already says on the phone. Those sentences are the draft.

The visitor who believes the programs are real will look for the people who run them. [How a nonprofit should write an about page](/blog/how-a-nonprofit-should-write-an-about-page) is the next piece, because names and roles matter only when they change the decision to give, join, or read.
